Stuff from the States 

 

Alabama - ASAA Bill Passes Legislature (HB 161): The House concurred to the Senate’s amendment to this bill and passed it on February 10. The Senate amendment added language providing that compliance with the bill’s proposed age verification requirements does not relieve an entities’ age verification requirements under any other laws. The bill has now moved on to Governor Ivey for action.

 

California - Record CCPA Settlement: California AG Bonta announced a record $2.75 million civil penalty in a settlement with Disney on Wednesday, resolving allegations that the company’s opt-out mechanisms were not effectuated across distinct devices and services connected to the consumer’s account. The settlement underscores that, if a consumer is logged in to their account, an opt-out (whether provided via a toggle, webform, or GPC) must be extended to all devices and services associated with that account (and, if the consumer is not logged in when they opt-out, the company must inform the consumer of how to fully effectuate their opt-out). The announcement does not include allegations that the company improperly sold or shared minors’ personal information, but the settlement includes a provision specifying that the company “shall continue to not” sell or share minors’ personal information without required consent. The focus on the ease of exercising consumer rights and the sufficiency of opt-out mechanisms continues a trend from the AG’s 2025 CCPA enforcement activity. 

 

Connecticut

  • CTDPA Amendments Incoming: In a joint press conference with Connecticut Attorney General Tong highlighting the AG’s most recent CTDPA enforcement report, Sen. Maroney (D) announced legislative priorities for this year, including banning the sale of geolocation data and updating the CTDPA’s definition of publicly available information. 
  • Latest Enforcement Report Highlights Youth Privacy & Sensitive Data Focus: The third-annual CTDPA Enforcement Report once again provides details on how Connecticut’s comprehensive privacy law is being enforced. This year’s edition emphasizes the importance of “protecting kids online,” as the youth privacy protections in 2023’s SB 3 went into effect in October 2024. The AG’s Office sent violation notices to: a messaging platform, alleging deficiencies with the company’s privacy notice and opt-out practices; a game provider, investigating the collection and use of children’s personal data by SDKs for targeting advertising; and a gaming studio, alleging deficiencies in the company’s privacy notice and consent processes. As part of a broader coalition, Connecticut sent a letter to AI software production and distribution companies asking for quality control and additional safeguards in their products. Other key topics highlighted in the report include health information, location data, and genetic data. 
  • Direct-to-Consumer Genetic Testing Bill Introduced (HB 5128): In the enforcement report, the CT Attorney General “urge[d] the legislature to adopt a standalone genetic data privacy law to ensure that Connecticut residents have the same protections as residents of other states that have enacted such laws.” The Joint Committee on General Law has responded, introducing a Genetic Information Privacy Act that would apply to companies offering genetic testing directly to consumers. 

 

Florida - New Enforcement Division to Scrutinize Data Sharing with Foreign Adversaries: The transfer of Americans’ personal data to “foreign adversaries,” “countries of concern,” or entities under the direction or control of either has come under fire in recent years. Last week, the Florida Attorney General announced a new enforcement division—the Consumer Harm from International Nefarious Actors (CHINA) Prevention Unit—to investigate the sharing of Floridians' personal data with companies who have ties to foreign adversaries. The new unit is already active, having sent a subpoena to clothing retailer Shein and highlighting medical device manufacturers as the next target. 

 

Georgia

  • AADC-Style Bill Introduced (SB 495): Sen. Harrell (D) introduced this bipartisan, AADC-style bill proposing robust online privacy and safety protections for both consumers and minors, similar to the protections established in Nebraska, Vermont, and South Carolina. This bill would prohibit covered entities from engaging in or using certain “high-risk” data practices or design features unless the consumer explicitly requests the practice or feature and the covered entity has implemented age assurance to determine that the user is not a minor (u18). The bill would also require covered entities to assess the risk that any new or materially changed design will cause compulsive use in minors and take certain prescribed steps if such risk is reasonably foreseeable, provide certain default settings to minors, offer minors an interface to control settings and data use related to algorithmic feeds, and prominently disclose certain information related to minors’ personal data use by the service. The bill would create a PRA in addition to Attorney General enforcement.
  • ASAA Bill Introduced (SB 467): Introduced by Sen. Cowsert (R), this bill proposes an App Store Accountability Act-style age assurance framework with a few divergences, including requirements for age verifying existing accounts, parental consent obligations for pre-installed apps, and the absence of application exemptions (a factor in the preliminary injunction analysis against Texas’ law).

 

Illinois

  • Five Comprehensive Privacy Bills Now in Play: Last Friday, Sen. Ventura (D) introduced SB 3890, which is the fifth comprehensive privacy bill introduced in the Land of Lincoln (competing with Virginia-style bills SB 3220, SB 3548, & HB 5221 and Minnesota-style bill SB 2875). This is a Minnesota-style comprehensive privacy bill that also includes a Delete Act that would require data brokers to register with the state annually and the state to establish an accessible deletion mechanism allowing consumers to submit one deletion request to all registered data brokers.
  • Age Signals Bills Introduced (SB 3977/HB 5511): Sen. Ellman (D) introduced this California-style age signals bill on February 6. Diverging from the California model, this bill would include additional requirements for developers, including requiring operators of covered platforms to implement certain default settings for known minors and restricting operators from providing “addictive feeds” to known minors without parental consent.

 

Kansas

  • AADC-Style Bill Introduced (SB 499): The Kansas Senate Committee on Federal and State Affairs introduced this AADC-style bill on February 9, which largely matches the requirements of the bill introduced in Georgia this week with additional requirements related to minor chatbot interactions.
  • ASAA Bill Passed Out of Committee (SB 372): This bill passed out of committee on February 12, and now moves on to the Senate Floor for consideration.

 

Maryland

  • MODPA Immigration Enforcement Amendment (SB 504): Sen. Lam (D) has introduced a broad MODPA amendment that would make several changes, including: Expanding the definition of “precise geolocation data” to include information identifying the specific location of a mobile device or a vehicle, not just a consumer; narrow the definition of “publicly available information” to include only information processed in accordance with restrictions placed on the information by the governmental entity; re-name “sensitive data” as “sensitive attribute” and define “sensitive data” as data that includes (or is processed to identify) a sensitive attribute; narrow the data-level exemption for the federal Driver's Privacy Protection Act; prohibit controllers from selling personal data if they knew or should have known that the purchaser seeks to use the personal data for immigration enforcement; narrow the exception for compliance with civil, criminal, or regulatory inquiries exclude immigration enforcement.
  • Autonomous Vehicle MODPA Amendment Introduced (SB 909): This bill would amend MODPA to apply to any person that collects personal data through the use or operation of a fully autonomous vehicle (motor vehicle equipped with a level 4 or 5 system as defined by the "Taxonomy and Definitions for Terms Related to Driving Automation Systems for On-Road Motor Vehicles”  published by the Society of Automotive Engineers International in April 2021). It would also add a new subtitle to the Transportation Article regulating fully autonomous vehicles. 
  • Three Data Broker Bills Introduced: Last week, Sen. Hester (D) introduced a data broker bill (SB 616) that would require data brokers to register with the state annually and to maintain a comprehensive information security program. This week, Del. Solomon (D) introduced a companion to Sen. Hester’s bill (HB 1220) and Del. Wu (D) introduced a similar but less detailed bill (HB 1089) (e.g., failing to define “direct relationship”). 

 

Maine - Comprehensive Privacy Bill Passes House (LD 1822): The Maine House passed a broad, Maryland-style bill with substantive data minimization requirements on February 10. This bill was carried over from the 2025 legislative session.

 

New Jersey - AADC-Style Bill Introduced (S3413/A4015): Introduced by Sen. Mukherji (D) on February 9, this bill would amend New Jersey’s comprehensive privacy law to incorporate AADC-style requirements similar to Nebraska and Vermont, and includes third-party audit requirements similar to South Carolina that covered online services would be required to publicly and prominently post on the service’s website.

 

Rhode Island - AADC-Style Bill Introduced (HB 762): Rep. Cotter (D) introduced this AADC-style bill on February 11. This bill includes a CPA/CTDPA-style duty of care and requires covered entities to conduct DPIAs, restrict certain processing activities, and implement high-level default privacy settings for known minors. 

 

South Carolina - AADC Challenged:  As expected, NetChoice has filed a challenge to the recently enacted South Carolina Age-Appropriate Code Design Act, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief on First Amendment grounds. NetChoice contends that the law violates the First Amendment in numerous ways. For example, NetChoice alleges that the law’s requirement for covered online services to exercise reasonable care in preventing harm to minors amounts to a content-based restriction on speech that is both over- and underinclusive in its regulation of content. NetChoice also argues that the law is preempted by both Section 230 and COPPA and that it is void for vagueness. For detailed analysis on the South Carolina AADC, see Daniel Hales’s blog post on the FPF website. 

 

Texas - Lawsuit Filed Under DTPA & SCOPE Act: Attorney General Paxton filed a lawsuit against Snap on February 11. In the complaint, the AG alleges that the company violated the DTPA by: (1) misrepresenting app age rating information in the App Store, (2) failing to disclose accurate and relevant information about app content and appropriateness to consumers, and (3) failing to disclose that the app is “addictive and contributes to compulsive or excessive use.” The AG further alleges that the company violated the SCOPE Act by: (1) failing to provide a commercially reasonable method for a parent or guardian to verify their identity, (2) sharing, disclosing, and selling known minors’ personal information without obtaining parental consent, and (3) failing to provide verified parents with tools required by the act allowing a parent to “supervise…the known minor’s use of a digital service.” Although some provisions of the SCOPE Act are enjoined, such as the content monitoring and age verification requirements, this lawsuit signals that the AG is still prioritizing enforcement of the provisions that remain in effect as litigation continues.  

 

Virginia - VCDPA Social Media & AI Amendment Passes Senate (SB 85): The Virginia Senate voted 40-0 to pass SB 85, a bill concerning social graph data processed by a social media platform, contextual data processed by an artificial intelligence model operator, and interoperability requirements for social media. The Senate amended the bill, adjusting the definition of artificial intelligence and adding a definition of operator (a person who makes an AI model available to others).

 

Wisconsin - AADC-Style Bill Introduced (SB 978): Sen Smith (D) introduced this Vermont-style AADC bill on February 6.  

 

Federal Happenings 

 

FTC Sends PADFAA Warning: The Protecting Americans’ Data from Foreign Adversaries Act (PADFAA) prohibits data brokers from making Americans’ sensitive personal data available to foreign adversaries or entities subject to the control of a foreign adversary. This week the FTC announced that it had sent warning letters to thirteen data brokers, reminding them of their requirements under PADFAA. The impetus for sending the letters was the agency’s observation that some of the recipients offered solutions regarding Americans’ status as a member of the Armed Forces, which is a category of sensitive data under the law. The letters “encourage” recipients to review their practices and ensure compliance with the law.
